entry.title: How Homebrew Works: The Ruby Architecture Behind brew’s Formula System

link.title: How Homebrew Works: The Ruby Architecture Behind brew’s Formula System

entry.content:
Type brew install ffmpeg on a fresh Mac and Homebrew will resolve, fetch and link a dependency tree that can span dozens of packages — in the right order, without asking you anything, without a lockfile. The order it picks, the artifacts it trusts, and the absolute paths it quietly rewrites all come from decisions encoded in the Ruby files under Library/Homebrew in the Homebrew/brew repository. That core is compact enough that a working developer can read all of it in an afternoon, which is rare for software with this much surface area, and it makes brew one of the better codebases to study if you maintain any installer, registry client, or dependency tool of your own.

The pain brew solves is not merely “install things”. It is three specific problems you hit the first time you manage more than one Mac or Linux box. First, dependency resolution: something must always exist before something else, and the ordering has to survive optional dependencies, recommended ones, and cycles. Second, formula versioning: postgres@14 and postgres@16 must coexist while brew upgrade still does the right thing for unversioned names. Third, install reproducibility: build from source on two machines and you get two compiler personalities; brew’s default is to pour a prebuilt, attested bottle and only fall back to compiling when no bottle matches your platform.

Those three problems are handled by three mostly-separate subsystems: a loader chain that turns a name into a Ruby class, a recursive dependency expander with an explicit cycle guard, and a bottle-first installer that treats compilation as the exception. The rest of this post walks the subsystems in the order your package actually travels through them.

Overview: from the install command through formula resolution, dependency expansion, download strategies, and the pour into the Cellar.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • InstallCmd, L13 parses the brew install invocation, auto-installs the tap a named formula belongs to, then hands off to the installer.
  • Formulary.factory, L788 is the single resolution entry point: a name, alias, path, or URI all funnel through one cached dispatch.
  • FromAPILoader, L706 short-circuits core-tap names into JSON-loaded classes, skipping the tap checkout entirely.
  • Formula, L89 is the DSL base class; every formula file in homebrew-core is a Ruby class inheriting from it.
  • Dependency.expand, L223 walks the dependency graph recursively, applying prune and skip filters and merging repeats.
  • DownloadStrategyDetector.detect, L12 maps a URL or a symbol onto exactly one strategy class.
  • CurlDownloadStrategy, L9 handles plain HTTPS downloads, resolving redirects and resuming partial files.
  • CurlGitHubPackagesDownloadStrategy, L7 fetches bottles as OCI artifacts from ghcr.io.
  • Keg#link, L526 finally symlinks the installed keg into HOMEBREW_PREFIX with per-directory rules.

Detail: the loader hierarchy, the SoftwareSpec model, the expand-and-merge dependency algorithm with its cycle guard, the strategy classes, and the pour/link/receipt storage layer.

Formulas are Ruby classes, not YAML

The first thing to internalize is that a formula is code, not data. formula.rb runs 5,532 lines on the branch this tour reads, and it defines the DSL every formula author touches. The convenience methods are thin delegates: url, L4500 forwards to the active stable spec, as do version, L4514 and bottle, L4574, while depends_on, L4821 and conflicts_with, L4954 register edges in metadata arrays. The spec objects themselves are SoftwareSpec, L17 instances holding the URL, checksums, and an optional bottle block, L177; a formula carries two of them, stable and head, exposed at L180 and L191.

The build hook is famously empty: def install; end, L3587 is a no-op that subclasses override with system "make", "install" style steps. Everything around it — checksum verification, unpacking, chdir into buildpath — is provided by the framework, which is why the average formula stays under fifty lines. Versioning rides the same class: versioned_formula?, L699 is literally name.include?("@"), and the whole node@20/node@22 pattern falls out of that one predicate. If you have read our Ruby source tour, the code style will feel familiar: Sorbet sig blocks, # typed: strict headers, and OS-specific behavior split into extend/os/mac and extend/os/linux override files rather than scattered conditionals.

From git taps to a JSON API

Resolution has two generations living side by side. The old one assumes taps are git checkouts under Library/Taps, parsed by FromTapLoader, L502 — still the path for third-party taps. The new one, used by default for homebrew/core, is a JSON API: API.fetch_json_api_file, L50 downloads formula.json into a local cache, API::Formula.fetch_api!, L128 triggers the refresh, and download_and_cache_data!, L141 rebuilds alias and rename indexes in a single pass over that file. all_formulae, L162 lazily initializes the whole thing on first lookup.

The loader hierarchy in formulary.rb (1,117 lines) is where the dispatch lives: a base FormulaLoader, L311 with specialized subclasses — FromBottleLoader, L377, FromPathLoader, L447, FromTapLoader, L502, FromKegLoader, L618, FromURILoader, L655, FromCacheLoader, L669, and FromAPILoader, L706 — each answering try_new queries. There are also two composite loaders worth knowing: FromNameLoader, L573, which subclasses the tap loader for plain names, and FormulaJSONContentsLoader, L759, which builds a formula class directly from JSON contents with no file involved at all. The API path is opt-out via no_install_from_api?, L712, which reads the HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_FROM_API environment switch. Formulary.factory, L788 caps it off with a factory cache keyed "name:#{ref}-#{spec}-#{alias_path}" so repeated lookups during one run are nearly free.

Dependency resolution: recursion with a guard rail

Dependency, L10 is a small edge object — a name, tags, options, and hidden or recommended state — and to_formula, L58 resolves it into a real formula when needed. The algorithm is Dependency.expand, L223, a class method defined under class << self: it pushes the dependent’s name onto an @expand_stack (L227), iterates the declared deps, and asks a filter block for one of three verdicts — prune, skip, or keep-but-stop-recursing — before recursing into each dependency’s own formula (L254). The stack is the cycle guard: a dependency loop is detected by name membership and simply skipped rather than crashing the install. Results are deduplicated by merge_repeats, L263, and the stack pops in an ensure block so exceptions cannot corrupt it.

The installer side consumes this: compute_dependencies, L703 turns the expanded set into an ordered plan, verify_deps_exist, L403 fails fast on unknown names, and install_dependency, L962 constructs one FormulaInstaller per dependency — the recursion you see in the terminal is literally a nested installer. When you force a source build and any dependency lacks a bottle, UnbottledError, L580 stops the run before half the tree is compiled.

Download strategies: one URL, many classes

download_strategy.rb is only 53 lines long, and almost all of it is a require list (L24 through L42) wiring the 19 strategy files that live in Library/Homebrew/download_strategy/. The brain is DownloadStrategyDetector.detect, L12: detect_from_url (L32) pattern-matches the URL — git hosts get GitDownloadStrategy, L9 with its shallow clone_repo, L279; ghcr.io hosts get the GitHub Packages subclass; everything else lands on CurlDownloadStrategy, L9, whose fetch, L40 resolves redirects and resumes partial downloads. VCS strategies share a common ancestor in VCSDownloadStrategy, L9.

A formula can also force a strategy with the :using symbol, but the choice is policed: HOMEBREW_CONTROLLED_STRATEGIES, L44 whitelists exactly the seven curl-family strategies a formula may select. Resources declared inside a formula (Resource, L14, fetched at L221) ride the same detector, which is how one formula pulls several unrelated tarballs and patches through one consistent integrity check.

From brew install to a linked keg: build facts from the tree

The install sequence ties everything together, and the code reads like a checklist. FormulaInstaller#install, L559 locks the formula (L560), runs build-from-source checks when no bottle can be poured (L563), checks conflicts (L578), computes and installs dependencies (L583, L591). Whether to pour is decided by pour_bottle?, L263; the Formula-side default is pour_bottle? = true (L1661) — pour unless a formula opts out.

The pour itself (pour, L1729) stages the Bottle, L8 tarball into the Cellar (Bottle#stage, L253), reloads the tab, stamps poured_from_bottle = true (L1762), persists it with tab.write, L1774, and then calls replace_placeholders_with_locations, L1787 to rewrite the absolute paths baked in at build time. The receipt is AbstractTab, L11 with FILENAME = "INSTALL_RECEIPT.json" (L18); the concrete Tab, L4 subclass adds formula-specific fields, and Tab.create, L94 plus from_file, L114 bracket its lifecycle. Downloads are queued up-front by enqueue_fetch, L1626 with a Sigstore attestation check attached (verify_bottle_attestation?, L1684) — bottles are verified before anything is unpacked. When pouring is not possible, the fallback path is equally explicit: build, L630 runs the formula’s install hook, then Tab.clear_cache and a cleanup pass wipe anything the build left behind. Linking is Keg#link, L526 in the 996-line keg.rb: an opt link pass (L531) followed by link_dir rules for etc, bin, sbin, include and share (L535 onward), each directory getting its own mkpath/skip policy — which is exactly why some config files land in /etc while binaries end up in bin. For scale: cmd/ holds 76 user-facing command files, dev-cmd/ another 70, and the 2,052-line installer swaps mac/linux behavior through extend/os overrides rather than inline if statements.

Honest Limits

Line numbers here come from main at commit b43c73f8 on 2026-11-18; brew lands hundreds of commits a month, so treat the anchors as a snapshot, not a stable API. Coverage is partial by design: casks have their own installer under Library/Homebrew/cask/, and services, livecheck, and the RuboCop suite are entirely out of scope. The pour flow described assumes standard ghcr.io bottles — mirror setups go through different relocation logic and are flagged with a warning in the code. Finally, FormulaInstaller is an internal class with no stability promise; if you script against it, pin the commit. One connection worth noting: because versioned formulae are just ordinary classes with an @ in the name, parallel Node.js installs on one machine fall out of the same machinery for free — no lockfile, no plugin, just naming.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Homebrew's Ruby core: formula classes, loader chains, download strategies, dependency expansion and the bottle pour into the Cellar.

entry.title: pnpm Architecture: How the Content-Addressable Store, Symlinked node_modules, and the Resolver Actually Work

link.title: pnpm Architecture: How the Content-Addressable Store, Symlinked node_modules, and the Resolver Actually Work

entry.content:
Every JavaScript developer knows the ritual: clone a project, run an install, and watch hundreds of megabytes land in node_modules — most of it duplicated bytes that already existed in the project next door. npm and Yarn traditionally solved dependency isolation by copying: every version of every package gets materialized, per project, on your disk. Ten repositories that depend on the same library store ten identical physical copies of it.

The second pain is quieter: phantom dependencies. Flat hoisting — copying every transitive package up to the top-level node_modules so the module resolver can find it — means your code can require() a package you never declared. It works locally and explodes in CI where versions shifted. pnpm’s answer is a stricter layout: only your declared dependencies are visible, and everything else is locked away where Node’s resolution algorithm (we traced that algorithm in the Node.js source) cannot reach it from your project’s root.

The third pain is speed, and it is mostly the first in disguise: installs spend their time re-verifying, re-extracting, and re-writing files already on disk. pnpm’s core bet is that “already installed” should be answerable with a hash lookup and an inode check, not a network round trip and 30,000 file copies. All three answers live in one place: the pnpm monorepo on GitHub. We sparse-checked out its most architecture-revealing packages and read the install machinery end to end. Everything below — every symbol, every line number — was verified against the actual main tree, not against documentation.

pnpm's install at a glance: resolve, store, import, link, hoist. Every node is a real function in the pnpm/pnpm monorepo; every edge is data we traced between them.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • [resolveNpm, L59](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/resolving/npm-resolver/src/resolveNpm.ts#L59) — the resolver entry: pick a registry per scope, try workspace packages, then the lockfile fast path, then the registry.
  • [pickPackageFromMeta, L46](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/resolving/npm-resolver/src/pickPackageFromMeta.ts#L46) — turns a packument into a concrete version, honoring publish-date and deprecated-version policies.
  • [peekLockedPackage, L411](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/resolving/npm-resolver/src/resolveNpm.ts#L411) — the speed trick: when the lockfile pins an integrity-checked tarball, read its manifest straight out of the local store and skip the registry entirely.
  • [createCafs, L94](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/store/cafs/src/index.ts#L94) — builds the content-addressable file store API: every blob addressed by its sha512 digest.
  • [contentPathFromHex, L21](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/store/cafs/src/getFilePathInCafs.ts#L21) — maps a digest to files/<2 chars>/<rest>, with an -exec suffix for executable files.
  • [writeBufferToCafs, L12](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/store/cafs/src/writeBufferToCafs.ts#L12) — exclusive-create blob writes so concurrent installs cannot clobber each other, plus in-place repair of corrupt blobs.
  • [createIndexedPkgImporter, L27](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/fs/indexed-pkg-importer/src/index.ts#L27) — chooses how files leave the store: reflink clone, hardlink, or copy; auto probes and remembers the winner.
  • [linkDirectDeps, L30](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/installing/linking/direct-dep-linker/src/linkDirectDeps.ts#L30) — symlinks each project’s direct dependencies into its node_modules.
  • [hoist, L40](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/main/pnpm11/installing/linking/hoist/src/index.ts#L40) — the optional, opt-in hoister for packages that genuinely need loose resolution.

The detail view: 34 functions across six groups. Follow the edges from resolver to store, store to importer, importer to linker, linker to hoister.

The Content-Addressable Store: sha512, Two-Character Fan-Out

When a tarball arrives, pnpm does not unpack it into node_modules. It walks every file, hashes it, and writes it into a machine-wide store under a path derived from that hash. The algorithm is not configurable at this layer: HASH_ALGORITHM (L38) is exported as a plain 'sha512', and addBufferToCafs (L129) computes the digest with crypto.hash(HASH_ALGORITHM, buffer, 'hex'). A comment right above it is refreshingly empirical: “Calculating the integrity of the file is surprisingly fast. 30K files are calculated in 1 second. Hence, from a performance perspective, there is no win in fetching the package index file from the registry.”

The address layout is a two-level fan-out: contentPathFromHex (L25) builds files/<first two hex chars>/<remaining chars>, and appends -exec when the file is executable — decided by modeIsExecutable (L8), a one-liner testing (mode & 0o111) !== 0. That split exists because hard links preserve the store file’s mode, so executables and non-executables must be physically distinct blobs. The same function carries a micro-optimization comment worth quoting: the path is built with template strings instead of path.join because it is “a hot path called ~30k times per cold install; avoiding path.join saves ~30ms per install.”

The write path is defensive in an instructive way. writeBufferToCafs (L12) keeps a per-path locker, then uses exclusive creation — writeFileExclusive (L30) opens with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, so if another process created the same content-addressed file concurrently, you get EEXIST rather than a silent overwrite. The EEXIST winner then verifies the file’s integrity instead of trusting it. And if an existing blob fails verification (a crash mid-write, disk corruption), overwriteFileInPlace (L139) truncates and rewrites the file under the same inode — the comment cites issue pnpm/pnpm#3445 and explains why: every hard link from every project’s node_modules shares that inode, so one in-place repair heals all of them at once. Temporary files are named with the process ID plus worker thread ID (pathTemp, L235) instead of random bytes.

From Store to node_modules: Clone, Hardlink, Copy

The store lives once per machine; node_modules is a projection of it. The projection is built by the indexed package importer, and the strategy is explicit: PackageImportMethod (L21) is the union 'auto' | 'hardlink' | 'copy' | 'clone' | 'clone-or-copy', defaulting to auto in the switch at L45. auto probes the filesystem: it tries a reflink clone first (createClonePkg, L193 uses the @reflink/reflink native addon on macOS and Windows, and COPYFILE_FICLONE_FORCE on Linux), then a hardlink, and falls back to copying — caching whichever strategy won so later packages skip the probing.

The workhorse is linkOrCopy (L345): a plain fs.linkSync per file, where EEXIST is treated as success, and a curious fallback comment admits that “in some VERY rare cases (1 in a thousand), hard-link creation fails on Windows” — so the code simply copies instead. Before linking at all, pkgLinkedToStore (L392) compares inode numbers between the target file and the store file: equal ino means the hard link already exists and the whole package import can be skipped. That single stats0.ino === stats1.ino check is why repeated installs are nearly free.

Whole-directory safety is handled by importIndexedDir (L67): try an exclusive mkdir and import straight into it; if it exists, build the package in a staging directory and commit it with an atomic rename (importWithStaging, L87). One subtle ordering rule: package.json is imported last, through the atomic importer, because a concurrent reader uses its presence as the completion marker.

Symlinks All the Way Down: The node_modules Layout

This is the part users actually see. Your node_modules/react is not a directory — it is a symlink into node_modules/.pnpm/react@19.1.0/node_modules/react, and the files inside that are hard links into the store. The symlink itself is created by symlinkDependency (L10), which calls symlinkDir after joining the alias into the modules directory. The direct-dep linker linkDirectDeps (L30) runs it for every workspace project and dedupes: a dependency already linked from the root is unlinked from sub-projects rather than duplicated (linkDirectDepsAndDedupe, L43).

Because only declared dependencies get a top-level symlink, undeclared transitive packages are invisible to your code — phantom dependencies are structurally impossible, not just discouraged. For teams that still need loose resolution, hoisting exists as an explicit opt-in. hoist (L40) walks the dependency graph (graphWalker, L5), sorts candidates by depth (hoistGraph, L238), and lets the first claimant win each alias. selectHoistedModulesDir (L8) shows the two destinations: private hoists go to node_modules/.pnpm/node_modules (visible to nested packages, not to your source), while public hoists land in node_modules itself. A newer option, virtualStoreType: global, goes further: one virtual store shared across projects, per the repo’s own docs.

One implementation note: pnpm itself is written in TypeScript; for the tooling side, see our TypeScript compiler internals tour.

The Resolver: From Specifier to Tarball

Everything above assumes pnpm already knows which version to install. Deciding that is the resolver’s job, and its first move is avoiding work. resolveNpm (L59) handles workspace: protocol specifiers before touching the network (L106), then the fast path at peekLockedPackageUnlessUpdating (L158) checks whether the lockfile’s current resolution is an integrity-pinned tarball; if so, peekLockedPackage (L411) reads the manifest from the local store. The comment above it explains the win plainly: “This avoids the expensive metadata fetch from the registry.”

When a registry fetch is unavoidable, pickPackageFromMeta (L46) applies the policies: it detects unpublished packages (UNPUBLISHED_PKG, L64), rejects metadata whose name mismatches the request, and delegates range resolution to pickVersionByVersionRange (L222), which prefers dist-tags.latest and deliberately uses loose semver so a * range can still match prerelease versions — the comment cites issue #865. Deprecated versions get one more chance at redemption: nonDeprecatedPick (L349) tries the same release line for a non-deprecated alternative before giving up. If nothing matches, NoMatchingVersionError (L11) surfaces the failure when neither the registry nor the workspace has a match.

From Copying Every File to Linking Once: Engineering Facts Worth Stealing

The repo’s own shape encodes its history. The TypeScript CLI and roughly sixty library packages live under pnpm11/, and pnpm-workspace.yaml documents a versioning band: while the CLI is on major 11, every library rides majors 1100–1199, bumped in lockstep so a consumer never mixes incompatible internals. STORE_VERSION is pinned to 'v11' at L9 of core/constants — store layouts change with majors, and the version suffix keeps an old binary from reading a store format it cannot parse. The default store path is <pnpm-home>/store/v11, but pnpm11/store/path probes the project’s drive first and falls back to <mountpoint>/.pnpm-store/v11, because hard links cannot cross volumes. And the story no longer ends at TypeScript: the same workspace file notes that the published npm pnpm package is now fronted by a thin Rust wrapper (the workspace package pacquet) that dispatches to per-platform binaries — a good segue into our Rust source tour.

The micro-decisions are just as transferable. Path construction in the store’s hottest function is hand-inlined to save ~30 ms per cold install. Hashing is trusted over network metadata because it measured faster. Temp files encode pid plus worker-thread ID instead of random bytes. Integrity verification runs in worker threads, with per-worker tallies handed back and summed by the main thread (the comment at L36 of checkPkgFilesIntegrity). None of these are glamorous; together they are why a warm install of thousands of packages finishes in seconds.

Honest Limits

This tour reads four packages deeply — store/cafs, fs/indexed-pkg-importer, resolving/npm-resolver, and installing/linking — out of a workspace listing dozens more under pnpm11/. The Rust wrapper (pacquet) and the pnpr experiment were not audited; statements about them come from pnpm-workspace.yaml comments, not their code. Line numbers refer to main as of today and will drift. Most diagram edges are direct calls, but a few (notably “blobs ready to import”) represent data flow between install stages rather than literal invocations. On exotic filesystems the code carries the most fallback comments; treat any single observed behavior as one branch of a larger decision tree.
entry.summary: How pnpm works under the hood: a sha512 content-addressable store, hard links into node_modules/.pnpm, strict symlinks, and the npm resolver, read from source.

entry.title: How uv Works: The Rust Architecture Behind Python’s Fastest Package Manager

link.title: How uv Works: The Rust Architecture Behind Python’s Fastest Package Manager

entry.content:
Every Python developer knows the ritual: create a virtualenv, upgrade pip, run pip install -r requirements.txt, then stare at the resolver as it backtracks through incompatible version combinations of your transitive dependencies. On projects with deep graphs — a data stack pulling in dozens of packages — resolution alone can stall for minutes, and none of that work is reused between runs. The cache misses, the wheels download again, and the interpreter churns through a parser built for a world where networks were slow.

uv is Astral’s answer to exactly this pain. It replaces the pip workflow — install, compile, sync, lock — with a single Rust binary that treats dependency resolution as a concurrent systems problem rather than a sequential script. Since its release it has spread rapidly through the Python ecosystem, and teams that adopted it mostly stayed: the speed is not a marketing veneer, it is structural, coming from how the resolver, the cache, and the installer are designed at the source level.

This post is a source-level tour of that design. We cloned the repository at commit 7f396534d583 on main and read the real code — every symbol and line number below is checked against the actual tree, not guessed. If you like Rust systems archaeology in the same spirit as ripgrep, this is a good one to follow along in a second terminal window.

uv's architecture on main: the CLI drives workspace discovery, a PubGrub resolver fed by an async registry client, and a planner that installs through the shared cache.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Resolver::resolve, L314 — the entry point that pairs a metadata-fetching future with the solver and joins them via tokio::try_join! (L344).
  • ResolverState, L131 — the shared state read by the solver, the fetcher, and the reporter.
  • MetadataRequests, L22 — metadata requests queued through an mpsc::channel(300) (resolver/mod.rs L321), sized deliberately to accommodate batch prefetching.
  • BatchPrefetcher, L44 — predicts which metadata the solver will need next and fetches it in batches before it is asked for.
  • PrioritizedDist, L26 — ranks compatible wheels and source distributions per version, including platform tag priority.
  • Cache, L162 — a versioned bucket layout (CacheBucket, L1042) with pruning that is hardlink-aware (L623).
  • CachedClient, L216 — wraps BaseClient and deserializes cached metadata zero-copy through the rkyv helpers in rkyvutil.rs (L25).
  • Lock, L313 — the lockfile writer, with format version 1 (L99) and revision 5 (L133) constants guarding compatibility.
  • create_venv, L81 — the tail of every install: write pyvenv.cfg, seed it, and link the environment.

The full resolution path in detail: request channel, prefetcher, fork handling, rkyv-backed cache layers, and the installer's link modes.

A Workspace of 91 Crates

uv is not one big Rust file; it is a disciplined Cargo workspace. The root Cargo.toml declares members = ["crates/*"] (L2) — which resolves to 91 crate directories — with resolver = "2" (L8), edition = "2024" (L11), and rust-version = "1.98.0" (L12). Exactly one crate, uv-trampoline, is excluded because it needs nightly (L6); it builds the tiny Windows launcher executables instead of relying on batch-script entry points.

The layering is strict. The uv binary crate contains only pub async fn run (crates/uv/src/lib.rs L134) and an unsafe fn main (L3077); the actual command tree lives in uv-cli, where Cli (L84), Commands (L345), and PipCommand (L788) are defined with clap. Settings are parsed into typed option structs — ResolverOptions (crates/uv-settings/src/settings.rs L662) and InstallerOptions (L561) — rather than passed around as loose config blobs.

The small crates at the bottom of the graph are where performance habits show. uv-performance-memory-allocator switches the global allocator to mimalloc on Windows and jemalloc elsewhere, selected per target architecture (lib.rs L1-L19). uv-small-str defines SmallString(ArcStr) (L10), a compact string representation for the millions of package names and versions flowing through a solve. uv-fastid generates identifiers as a raw Id([u8; 16]) (L20) instead of heap-allocated UUID strings. None of these are glamorous, but together they cut allocation churn from the hot path.

The Resolver: PubGrub on a Dedicated Thread

The heart of uv is crates/uv-resolver. The Resolver generic struct (L124) carries two pluggable pieces — a ResolverProvider for metadata and an InstalledPackagesProvider for the current environment — while ResolverState (L131) holds everything mutable. When resolve starts, it does something unusual: it spawns the PubGrub solver on a dedicated OS thread explicitly named uv-resolver (L328-L333) and runs the metadata fetcher as an async task concurrently, joining both with try_join!. Solving is CPU-bound pointer chasing; fetching is IO-bound. Separating them means neither starves the other.

The solver itself is not a hand-rolled SAT search. uv imports a fork of the PubGrub crate — the workspace pins pubgrub 0.7.1 as the package astral-pubgrub with an unstable-state-api feature (Cargo.toml L229) — and adapts it through UvDependencyProvider (dependency_provider.rs L15). Inside solve (L353) you can see the machinery: a FxHashSet of visited packages (L366), State::init of the PubGrub machine (L369), a BatchPrefetcher (L370), and a ForkState whose incompatibility arena is taken out and reused across branches (L378). Forks — uv’s mechanism for branching the solve when a package needs contradictory versions — are tracked in ForkMap (fork_map.rs L16), a plain FxHashMap<PackageName, Vec<Entry<T>>> with a unit-typed ForkSet alias (L12).

Selection policy is separated from the search. VersionMap (version_map.rs L34) decides which versions are candidates for a package given the Python target; PrioritizedDist (prioritized_distribution.rs L26) ranks the compatible wheels and sdists within a version, with a wheel-compatibility variant carrying an explicit tag priority (L460-L493); and AllowedYanks (yanks.rs L14) encodes whether yanked releases may still be selected. This separation is what lets uv implement resolution modes and preferences without tangling them into the solver.

The Cache: Hardlink-Aware and Zero-Copy

uv’s cache is the reason a second sync feels instantaneous. Cache (crates/uv-cache/src/lib.rs L162) organizes disk under versioned CacheBucket directories (L1042) — the doc comments show concrete layouts like wheel-metadata-v0/pypi/foo/foo-1.0.0-py3-none-any.msgpack — so a cache format change invalidates only one bucket instead of everything. The prune logic is unusually careful: “Remove file objects with no hardlinks outside the files bucket” (L623-L626), counting references with uv_fs::hardlink_count (L640) before deleting, because installed environments may still point into the cache.

Networking goes through RegistryClient (crates/uv-client/src/registry_client.rs L275), whose simple_detail (L403) fetches PyPI Simple API index pages, built on BaseClient (base_client.rs L766) configured by BaseClientBuilder (L109) for retries, proxies, and TLS. Cached responses are handled by CachedClient — literally a one-field tuple struct around BaseClient (L216) — whose Cacheable trait supports both serde and rkyv (L30-L38). The rkyv path is the interesting one: rkyvutil.rs defines the Serializer (L25) and Deserializer (L36) aliases so cached metadata can be read without deserializing into owned Rust types. On top of that sits a real HTTP caching layer implementing RFC 9111 semantics — revalidation (httpcache/mod.rs L386), Vary handling (L192) — and when a project lacks PEP 658 metadata files, uv falls back to reading metadata from remote zip central directories (wheel_metadata_from_remote_zip, remote_metadata.rs L49). Credentials are memoized in CredentialsCache (crates/uv-auth/src/cache.rs L35).

From Backtracking to Batch Prefetch: Build Facts in Numbers

A few concrete engineering facts from the tree, for readers who like numbers:

  • The metadata channel between fetcher and solver is mpsc::channel(300) — the comment (resolver/mod.rs L320) says the size is set large specifically to accommodate batch prefetching. Prefetching exists because PubGrub explores in a breadth-ish order the fetcher cannot predict one request at a time.
  • The lockfile format is version 1 with revision 5 (const VERSION, L99; const REVISION, L133 in lock/mod.rs), and the revision history is documented in place (L126-L132): revision 2 added upload times, 3 added per-package exclude-newer, 5 added default-group metadata. Older files with revision = 3 still read correctly.
  • LinkMode (crates/uv-fs/src/link.rs L26) has exactly four variants — Clone, Copy, Hardlink, Symlink — and the default is Clone on macOS and Linux (APFS, btrfs, xfs, bcachefs support copy-on-write) and Hardlink elsewhere (L15-L17, L39-L51). Installs are therefore usually reflinks or hardlinks into cache-owned files, not byte copies.
  • The install planner, Planner::build (crates/uv-installer/src/plan.rs L291), partitions work into cached distributions, remote downloads, and reinstalls (see the pushes at L419, L453, L462), and Installer::install (installer.rs L102) has a synchronous twin install_blocking (L146).
  • Interpreter discovery — how uv finds the CPython interpreters it will build environments on, including its own managed downloads — lives in find_python_installations (crates/uv-python-discovery/src/discovery.rs L922), with the resulting Interpreter value modeled in uv-python-interpreter (interpreter.rs L51).

Installs, LinkMode, and Virtualenvs

Once the plan exists, the installer walks it. Cached distributions are materialized through install_wheel (crates/uv-install-wheel/src/install.rs L53), which unpacks wheel payloads into site-packages using uv-fs (declared as a workspace dependency in uv-install-wheel’s Cargo.toml, L24) — that is where LinkMode actually gets exercised file by file. Environment creation is create_venv (crates/uv-virtualenv/src/lib.rs L81), which writes pyvenv.cfg, records a seed setting (virtualenv.rs L580-L582, with the Seed enum at L731), and on Windows installs trampoline executables instead of Python-script launchers (L294). Workspaces — uv’s monorepo feature — are discovered by walking upward through pyproject.toml files, a procedure documented step by step above Workspace::discover (crates/uv-workspace/src/workspace.rs L447-L463), with a dedicated WorkspaceCache so repeated discovery does not re-read every member manifest (L152-L160).

Honest Limits

This is a static source tour, not a benchmark: we verified structures, algorithms, and constants in the tree at commit 7f396534d583, but no end-to-end timings were measured for this post, and uv’s own performance claims live in its benchmarks documents rather than in code. Line numbers will drift as main moves — the resolver file alone is several thousand lines and changes weekly. The diagrams necessarily flatten nuance: pubgrub/mod.rs is a thin re-export module over Astral’s forked crate, and the fork/arena logic inside resolver/mod.rs spans thousands of lines we compressed into two nodes. Finally, uv is moving fast — the lockfile revision, the resolver’s fork machinery, and the workspace discovery rules have all changed in recent months, so treat this as a snapshot of a healthy, actively evolving codebase, not a frozen specification.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of uv: the PubGrub resolver, rkyv-backed cache, hardlink installs, and virtualenv engine that make Python packaging fast.

entry.title: How AppFlowy Works: Inside the Rust and Flutter Notion Alternative

link.title: How AppFlowy Works: Inside the Rust and Flutter Notion Alternative

entry.content:
Your Notion workspace lives on Notion’s servers. Offline mode is limited, sync is a black box, and if their API or pricing changes, your carefully linked databases go with it. AppFlowy — the AGPL-licensed open-source Notion alternative — takes the opposite trade: the same kind of workspace, but the backend is a Rust library compiled into your app, documents are CRDT files on your own disk, and the server is strictly optional. The whole thing is one repository you can clone and read.

This post walks the AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy source at its main branch with two generated architecture diagrams. The first is a 12-node overview that follows the stack from Flutter widgets down to SQLite. The second is a 32-node detail map of the pieces that actually matter: the FFI bridge, the event dispatcher, the eight domain plugins, the yrs CRDT layer, and the optional AppFlowy Cloud sync. Every node in the SVGs links to the real file on GitHub, and every symbol quoted below was verified against the tree at commit time.

By the end you’ll know how a keystroke in the editor becomes a protobuf event, crosses dart:ffi into Rust, gets routed to one of eight plugins, lands in either Diesel-managed SQLite or a yrs CRDT document, and — only if you opted in — syncs over a WebSocket. If you’ve followed our earlier source tours of Rust codebases or TypeScript web apps, this one is interesting precisely because it refuses to be a web app.

Overview: the Flutter UI talks protobuf over FFI to the Rust core, which routes events through plugins into SQLite and the yrs collab layer, with cloud sync as a detachable group on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The root container is one struct. AppFlowyCore, L61 holds managers for users, folder, documents, databases, search, AI and storage, plus the event_dispatcher and a server_provider. Its init at AppFlowyCore::new, L86 assembles every dependency before the UI renders a single widget.
  • The Dart side boots Rust first. InitRustSDKTask, L13 serialises paths, device id and cloud config into a JSON AppFlowyConfiguration, and FlowySDK.init, L37 registers two Dart ports before calling init_sdk natively.
  • There is exactly one C entry point for startup. init_sdk, L114 parses that JSON, spawns a dedicated OS thread running a Tokio runtime inside a LocalSet, and constructs the whole AppFlowyCore there.
  • Everything after startup is request/response over FFI. Dart’s Dispatch.asyncRequest, L53 writes a protobuf request to bytes, allocates an FFI buffer, and hands over a completion port; Rust’s async_event, L175 picks it up and posts the response bytes back to the same port.
  • One dispatcher, no routing framework. AFPluginDispatcher, L63 keeps a map of plugins and, via async_send, L79, finds whichever plugin registered the event id on the request.
  • Eight plugins cover the whole product. make_plugins, L12 returns user, folder, database, document, date, search, AI and file-storage plugins — and each one takes only Weak references to the managers, so the dispatcher never owns domain state.
  • Events are protobuf enums, not strings. DocumentEvent, L59 declares 21 numbered events from CreateDocument = 0 to GetDocumentText = 20, each with typed protobuf input and output declared via derive macros.
  • Metadata lives in SQLite under Diesel. init, L32 opens flowy-database.db (named at DB_NAME, L30) and runs embedded Diesel migrations on every launch.
  • Content lives in CRDT collabs, not SQLite. AppFlowyCollabBuilder, L76 builds one yrs-backed Collab per document, grid or board, flushed to disk by write_collab_to_disk, L363.

Detail: the full round trip — Dart launch tasks and blocs, the generated FFI bindings, the Rust dispatch loop, the plugin registries, the managers behind them, and the collab/cloud groups where edits become CRDT updates.

The Rust core: one dispatcher, eight plugins

frontend/rust-lib is a Cargo workspace of ~25 crates: lib-dispatch is the event bus, flowy-core is the composition root, and the rest are domain crates (flowy-folder, flowy-document, flowy-database2, flowy-user, flowy-ai, flowy-search, flowy-storage) plus plumbing (flowy-error, flowy-sqlite, dart-ffi). The plugin model is refreshingly small: AFPlugin, L64 is a name, a state (the manager as Weak), and a list of handlers bound with an .event() builder at .event, L107. Registration reads like a table of contents: the folder plugin wires ~45 handlers from FolderEvent, L66 (view creation, moving nested views, trash, favorites), the database plugin from DatabaseEvent, L11 (fields, rows, cells, filters, sorts), the document plugin from DocumentEvent above.

Two details make this design hold up. First, errors are uniform: every handler returns FlowyResult<T>, where FlowyError, L17 wraps a numeric ErrorCode, L10 that survives the FFI hop as protobuf. Second, handlers never reach each other directly — the document plugin asks the database plugin’s manager through resolved dependencies in flowy-core/src/deps_resolve/, keeping the event graph acyclic. This is the same “thin framework, fat domain crates” pattern we liked in our Rust tour at /rust/, just with a Flutter front door.

The Dart side: protobuf bytes over dart:ffi

AppFlowy does not use method channels for its event traffic. The generated ffi.dart looks up async_event directly in libdart_ffi, and dispatch.dart does the wire format by hand: request.writeToBuffer() (protobuf), a calloc.allocate buffer, and ffi.async_event(port.nativePort, input, bytes.length) at dispatch.dart, L130. On the Rust side the bytes become an AFPluginRequest, the Runner loop spawns it as a local task, and the response goes back through post_to_flutter, L258, which posts FFI-encoded bytes onto the allo_isolate port Dart is awaiting.

That mechanism also runs backwards, continuously. FlowySDK.init registers a stream port at set_stream_port, L38, and Rust pushes notifications — document changes, sync state, user events — through a registered NotificationSender (register_notification_sender, L22). The Flutter layer is then classic flutter_bloc: DocumentBloc, L47 owns one open document, throttles selection sync at 250 ms, and funnels editor transactions into the same dispatch round trip. Every Dart call site is generated per module — dispatch.dart literally parts in dart_event/flowy-*/dart_event.dart files that mirror the Rust event maps, which is why adding an event means touching both sides and regenerating.

Where your data lands: SQLite for metadata, CRDT for content

AppFlowy splits persistence deliberately. Relational, queryable state — user profiles, workspace/view metadata, KV preferences — goes to SQLite through Diesel 2.1 (diesel with sqlite and r2d2 pool features at Cargo.toml, L75). Migrations are compiled into the binary (MIGRATIONS, L29) and applied in init before any handler runs, so a user upgrading the app always lands on the current schema. The per-user connection comes straight from the user session — get_sqlite_db, L370.

Document content never touches those tables. Each document, grid, board or calendar is a yrs CRDT whose updates are encoded and flushed by CollabPersistenceImpl (CollabPersistenceImpl, L417): write_collab_to_disk encodes the doc, then flush_doc writes the state vector and doc state inside one transaction (flush_doc, L384). DocumentManager keeps open documents in a DashMap<Uuid, Arc<RwLock<Document>>> at DocumentManager, L54, with open_document at open_document, L327. Undo/redo is a CRDT feature: collab.enable_undo_redo() is called when a document collab is built (enable_undo_redo, L169), which is why undo survives restarts. If you want the general pattern — when to keep data in SQLite versus beside it — we cover it in the SQLite post at /sqlite/.

Sync: yrs CRDT updates over an optional WebSocket

The local-first claim is enforced in code, not marketing. A workspace is either local or cloud — DocumentBloc checks WorkspaceTypePB.LocalW at isLocalMode, L102, and the Dart auth layer picks BackendAuthService(AuthTypePB.Local) versus AppFlowyCloudAuthService in one switch at currentCloudType, L107. With local auth, no network client is even constructed.

When you do enable sync, the pieces are conventional but cleanly separated. AppFlowyCloudServer::new at AppFlowyCloudServer, L62 builds a REST client (base URL, WebSocket URL, Auth0-style gotrue_url at AFCloudClient::new, L76) and the WSClient::new, L91 WebSocket client; spawn_ws_conn at spawn_ws_conn, L97 re-establishes the socket as tokens refresh. Open documents get one WebSocketChannel per object id via collab_ws_channel, L245. The CRDT engine itself is yrs, L98 — the Rust port of Yjs — pinned at 0.21.0, and finalize() attaches cloud sync plugins to a collab only when sync_enable is set (finalize plugins, L341). Because edits merge as CRDT updates rather than OT on a central server, offline edits replay cleanly when the socket returns.

From a TypeScript web app to a Flutter-first repo

One structural fact worth knowing before you dig in: earlier AppFlowy versions carried an in-tree TypeScript web client, but today’s main branch contains no package.json anywhere — the web frontend is no longer part of this repository, and the entire shipped frontend is the Flutter app plus the Rust workspace. That makes the repo unusual among Notion alternatives: instead of “web app first, Electron shell later”, every desktop and mobile target compiles the same Dart UI against the same native Rust library (README lists macOS, Windows and Linux downloads plus App Store and Play Store listings). The cost is visible in the numbers: git ls-tree -r HEAD on main counts ~2,700 files under frontend/appflowy_flutter and ~950 under frontend/rust-lib, with generated protobuf Dart under packages/appflowy_backend/lib/protobuf acting as the contract between them. If you are porting a web-first product, the TypeScript archives on this blog show the pattern AppFlowy moved away from — and the diagrams above show what a native-first split looks like instead.

Honest Limits

  • sync_event is a stub. The synchronous FFI entry point logs unimplemented sync_event and returns empty bytes at sync_event, L230 — every real interaction takes the async path, so there is no synchronous escape hatch for tools embedding the core.
  • Conflict handling admits gaps. The document bloc’s own comment says the logic “is not fully implemented yet” and forces state reloads via a sync timer (conflict comment, L98). CRDTs merge text reliably, but UI-level conflict UX is still defended with timers.
  • Undo/redo is not uniform across object types. It is enabled for document collabs at creation (enable_undo_redo above), but the folder builder path (create_folder, L200) does not enable it, so workspace-tree edits behave differently from document edits.
  • The AGPL core and the cloud are different codebases. The README pins this repo to AGPL-3.0 (license badge, L16); the server that powers AppFlowy Cloud sync lives elsewhere, so self-hosting the full stack means deploying a second project.
  • Everything above reflects main on 2026-11-17 — commit-verified line numbers, not documentation. AppFlowy moves fast; treat exact line anchors as a snapshot.
entry.summary: How AppFlowy works inside: the Rust event dispatcher, Dart FFI, Diesel SQLite storage, yrs CRDT sync and plugin system of the open-source Notion alternative.

entry.title: How Baserow Works: Inside the Open-Source Airtable Alternative

link.title: How Baserow Works: Inside the Open-Source Airtable Alternative

entry.content:
Your team hits it every quarter: the Airtable base that runs operations crosses its API rate limit, automation scripts start failing with 429s, and the export button offers you a ZIP of CSVs instead of a database. The rows live in a proprietary cloud, the schema you carefully built cannot be reached with plain SQL, and pricing scales with collaborators rather than with data. Baserow attacks exactly that pain: it is the open-source, self-hostable Airtable alternative where every “base” is a real Postgres schema you own, every row is a real row, and the grid workflow your team already knows runs on infrastructure you control.

This post walks through Baserow’s source (the develop branch of baserow/baserow) with two architecture diagrams. The overview diagram traces the full loop of one request: the Nuxt frontend calls the Django REST API, registries dispatch the work to plugins, a runtime-generated Django model turns it into SQL against Postgres, and Redis fans the resulting change back out to every connected browser. The detail diagram zooms into the four mechanisms that make that loop possible: the field type plugin contract, the dynamic model engine, the view/filter layer, and the websocket broadcast path.

By the end you will know how a click in the grid becomes a SQL statement, how Baserow manufactures Django models at runtime for tables users created seconds ago, what a field type plugin must implement, and how an edit in Berlin shows up in a colleague’s browser in Tokyo without any polling. All line references point into the real repository, so you can click through and verify every claim.

Baserow overview architecture: the browser talks to a Django REST API; field and view plugins feed the dynamic model engine that maps every table onto Postgres, and a Redis-backed websocket layer pushes changes back to the client.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A database is just one application type. Baserow’s core layer manages workspaces, and a “database” is a pluggable application attached to one. Database, L80 extends the shared Application model, so permissions, trash and templates behave identically across application kinds.
  • Every column is a plugin instance. The FieldType contract, L100 defines what a field must implement, and FieldTypeRegistry, L2689 resolves type strings like text or link_row to those plugins. At startup, field registration, L241 registers the whole catalog.
  • Plugins mint real Django columns. TextFieldType.get_model_field, L529 returns an actual models.TextField(...) — the same class you would type by hand — so a user-created “Name” column becomes a genuine Postgres column.
  • A table manufactures its own model. Table.get_model, L1012 builds a temporary Django model per table: a unique uuid app label for thread safety at L1081, and a Meta.db_table binding at L1105 that points at the physical database_table_<id> table named by USER_TABLE_DATABASE_NAME_PREFIX, L2.
  • Generated models are cached, not rebuilt. generated_models_cache, L31 stores the manufactured field attributes in Redis keyed by table id and Baserow version, and a pre-migrate hook clears the whole cache at L1425.
  • Row work flows through the manufactured model. RowHandler.get_rows, L2819 and RowHandler.create_row, L792 are plain Django ORM operations against the generated model — no bespoke SQL layer, which is why filters and sorts compose naturally.
  • Views are query decorators, not separate storage. ViewHandler.apply_filters, L1915 folds the active view’s filters and sorts into the row queryset. The open-source view catalog is exactly three plugins — GridViewType, L79, GalleryViewType, L390 and FormViewType, L627 — registered at L407, each persisting its options in typed models such as GridView, L603.
  • Edits fan out through Redis, not polling. Handlers broadcast through PageType.broadcast, L116 scoped by TablePageType, L24, the events travel over the RetryingRedisChannelLayer, L63 wired in as the Django Channels backend at CHANNEL_LAYERS, L285, and the browser’s RealTimeHandler, L25 keeps one reconnecting WebSocket alive to patch the Vue stores.

Baserow internals: the generic registry pattern, the four jobs of a field type plugin, the get_model → GeneratedTableModel → Redis cache engine, the view/filter layer, and the broadcast path from handler to browser store.

Why the Table Model Is Built at Runtime

Django models are Python classes resolved at import time, but Baserow’s core product is letting end users create tables long after the server booted. A static models.py cannot know that a customer will add a “Churn Risk” table on Tuesday afternoon. Baserow therefore manufactures the model on demand: Table._get_model, L1025 documents itself as “Generates a temporary Django model based on available fields”, and the construction is exactly the type() dance every Django developer has seen in metaprogramming tutorials — attributes dict, Meta inner class, app label.

Two details show the engineering care. First, each generation gets a unique app label built from a uuid4 at L1081 so two threads building models for the same table never collide in Django’s global app registry. Second, the Meta at L1105 sets ordering to ["order", "id"] and creates a composite index on (order, id) at L1091 — the trick that makes drag-to-reorder rows an index scan instead of a table sort. Cross-table link_row relations are handled with a many-to-many model cache threaded through the generation call at L1054 to break the recursion that appears when two tables reference each other.

This is the same dynamic-model technique that powers Django itself under the hood — Baserow just industrialises it: one model per user table, per request path, cached aggressively in between.

The FieldType Contract: One Plugin, Four Jobs

Open field_types.py and you find 32 FieldType classes in one file, from TextFieldType, L506 to FormulaFieldType, L6675. The base contract at FieldType, L100 forces each plugin to answer four distinct questions:

  1. API shape — get_serializer_field builds the DRF serializer that validates incoming JSON; TextFieldType constructs a CharField with the configured default and max length at L516.
  2. Storage — get_model_field returns the Django column: models.TextField for text at L529, a decimal-aware field for NumberFieldType, L1273, a through-model relation for LinkRowFieldType, L3137.
  3. Query behaviour — methods like contains_query and starts_with_query at L541 teach the filter system what SQL each operator means for this type; that is how the view layer stays type-agnostic.
  4. Formula integration — to_baserow_formula_type at L550 declares how the type participates in Baserow’s formula language, which is also how FormulaFieldType, L6675 computes values from other columns.

FieldHandler.create_field, L285 dispatches through the registry by type string, alters the Postgres schema via the plugin’s column definition, and invalidates the generated model. The consequence is Baserow’s most valuable architectural property: adding a new column type — a rating field, a phone field, a duration field — is one new subclass plus one registration line, with zero edits to the row engine or the view layer. Every downstream mechanism consumes plugins through the same generic Registry, L763 base that all of Baserow’s plugin systems share.

Views as Plugins: Grid, Gallery, Form

A view in Baserow is not a copy of the data; it is a saved set of decorators over one shared row stream. The open-source core registers exactly three: grid, gallery and form (see the registration at L407). GridViewType, L79 carries the spreadsheet behaviour — filters, aggregations, ordering — while GalleryViewType, L390 renders the same rows as cards and FormViewType, L627 exposes a public submission surface that writes rows. Options live in typed Django models like GridView, L603, so a view survives restarts and exports cleanly.

When rows are fetched, ViewHandler.apply_filters, L1915 asks each filter’s field type for its query method and folds everything into one queryset — the grid, the gallery and a REST API caller can therefore share identical filter semantics without duplicating logic. On the client, the rendering is a Node-powered Nuxt/Vue application (web-frontend/nuxt.config.ts), whose per-concern stores in web-frontend/modules/database/store/ — field.js, view.js, table.js — are the landing zone for realtime patches rather than re-fetching the world on every change.

From Postgres DDL to Live Cells: Build Facts You Can Verify

Every user table is a real Postgres table named database_table_<id> (constants, L2). TableHandler.create_table, L364 creates it together with its first fields via create_table_and_fields, L432, which means psql access to your own data is guaranteed by construction, not by an export feature.

A few more facts you can check directly in the tree: the manufactured class is named Table<id>Model (L1006); the Redis cache entry key embeds the Baserow version (full_table_model_<id>_<version> at L34) so an upgrade can never serve a stale model; the channel layer serialises websocket payloads with a compressed MsgPack codec (L23) to cut Redis memory per broadcast; and the ws module ships event history and replay machinery (ws/history.py, ws/replay.py, plus migrations 0002_realtime_event_indexes and 0003_realtime_event_history), which is what lets a browser that dropped offline catch up on reconnect. The generated model itself defaults to managed=False (L1033) — Baserow owns the schema lifecycle through its own schema editor instead of Django migrations, which is why the pre-migrate signal clears the model cache.

Honest Limits

  • The view catalog is deliberately small in OSS. Core registers exactly three view types; richer visualisations live in the premium/ and enterprise/ trees of the same repository, so the open-source grid is the full picture only if you ignore those directories.
  • Plugin registration is boot-time only. All field and view types are registered during AppConfig.ready() (L241), so adding a field type is a Python restart, not a hot plugin load.
  • Realtime is Redis-dependent. Connection defaults live in settings, L174; a self-hosted deployment without Redis loses live sync, though REST still works.
  • The client trusts reconnect, not a queue. The browser’s delayedReconnect, L246 retries the socket on drop, and correctness during downtime rests on the server-side replay tables noted above — there is no client-side event buffer.
entry.summary: How Baserow works inside: Django field type plugins, runtime Django models over Postgres, and Redis websocket sync in the open-source Airtable alternative.

entry.title: How BookStack Works: Inside the Laravel Wiki Architecture

link.title: How BookStack Works: Inside the Laravel Wiki Architecture

entry.content:
Confluence bills per seat, hides its best features behind paid tiers, and somehow still feels slow on a five-person team. Notion locks your notes in a proprietary cloud. MediaWiki is powerful but overkill for internal docs. BookStack is the counter-offer: a free, self-hosted wiki built on the Laravel framework, MIT-licensed, with content organized the way humans actually think — Books hold Chapters, Chapters hold Pages. One PHP app, one MySQL database, no JavaScript framework required to understand it. That simplicity is exactly why its source code is worth reading.

We cloned the development branch of BookStackApp/BookStack and traced how each request really flows. The two diagrams below were generated directly from the repository structure — every node links to the actual source file on GitHub, so you can click through while reading.

By the end of this tour you will know how BookStack stores page content in three formats at once (HTML, Markdown and plain text), why it abandoned MySQL FULLTEXT for a hand-rolled scored index, how it avoids permission checks that recurse up the hierarchy on every query, and how one PageRepo::update() call fans out into revisions, search indexing, reference tracking and audit logs.

Overview of BookStack's architecture: controllers delegate to repositories, repositories shape content into three Eloquent models, and every listing is filtered through the permission engine and the scored search index.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • HTTP entry is one flat file. Nearly every page route lives in routes/web.php, L34, wrapped in a single Route::middleware('auth')->group(...) — there is no per-module routing magic to decode.
  • Controllers are thin on purpose. PageRepo, L44 shows getNewDraftPage() doing the real work: forcing draft => true, stamping ownership, and assigning the editor from PageEditorType::getSystemDefault, L32.
  • The hierarchy is three Eloquent models, not nested sets. Book, L51 declares pages() as a plain hasMany, Book, L68 adds chapters(), and Chapter, L30 orders its pages by a priority column. No materialized path, no closure table — just book_id and chapter_id foreign keys.
  • Every page row carries three content columns. Page, L31 extends the abstract BookChild, L15 and its docblock lists html, markdown and text properties plus a revision_count.
  • Dual editors converge on one normalizer. PageContent::setNewHTML, L40 stores HTML and blanks the Markdown column at L52, while setNewMarkdown, L58 converts through CommonMark at L62 — so rendering never has to care which editor wrote the page.
  • Permissions are pre-computed, not recursed. JointPermissionBuilder::rebuildForAll, L32 truncates a cache table and re-derives visibility per role, chunking books five at a time at L40.
  • Listings filter through that cache. PermissionApplicator::restrictEntityQuery, L99 attaches a whereHas('jointPermissions', ...) with a havingRaw status check at L108 — one subquery replaces tree-walking in PHP.
  • Search is a scored term table. SearchIndex::indexEntity, L35 deletes and re-inserts terms with weights, and SearchRunner, L191 joins that subquery back onto entities sorted by score.
  • Revisions are eager, not lazy. RevisionRepo::storeNewForPage, L19 snapshots name, HTML, Markdown, text and slug on every qualifying save.

The detailed view adds the collaboration layer: activity logging with queued webhooks, theme-event hooks fired during content conversion, and the three-engine PDF export path.

The Book → Chapter → Page Hierarchy Is Just Foreign Keys

BookStack’s data model refuses to be clever. Book is a container with hasMany relations to both Page and Chapter (Book, L51, L68); a Page may point at a chapter_id or sit directly under a book via directPages() at Book, L59. Shelves sit above books as a plain pivot: Book::shelves, L76 uses belongsToMany through bookshelves_books. Ordering within a book is handled by getDirectVisibleChildren() at Book, L84, which concatenates pages and chapters and sorts by priority — a manual, deterministic ordering scheme that makes drag-and-drop sort trivial to persist. URL slugs are regenerated on rename by BaseRepo::refreshSlug() at BaseRepo, L168, with a SlugHistory table catching old links.

One Save Flow Serves Both WYSIWYG and Markdown Editors

BookStack ships three editors — the enum at PageEditorType, L7 defines WysiwygTinymce = 'wysiwyg', WysiwygLexical = 'wysiwyg2024' and Markdown = 'markdown', with isHtmlBased() at L13 deciding which column wins. The branching happens in PageRepo::updateTemplateStatusAndContentFromInput(): markdown input forces the Markdown editor and routes through setNewMarkdown() at PageRepo, L170, while HTML input resolves the editor through a fallback chain ending in WysiwygTinymce at L174. Switching editors is a guarded permission (userCan(Permission::EditorChange)) at L178, and the choice is persisted per page in the editor column — not per session. Markdown conversion is not a regex toy: MarkdownToHtml::convert, L23 builds a league/commonmark environment with table, task-list and custom strikethrough extensions, and hands it to theme code at L30 before rendering. Even base64-pasted images are extracted and re-uploaded by extractBase64ImagesFromHtml() at PageContent, L77 so pages never embed megabyte data URIs.

Permissions Are a Materialized Cache, Not a Runtime Walk

This is the most instructive subsystem in the codebase. A naive wiki would check “does this role allow view on the page? if not, the chapter? if not, the book?” on every row. BookStack instead materializes the answer. Role-level rules live in EntityPermission rows (queried with a role_id = 0 fallback in PermissionApplicator, L80), and JointPermissionBuilder flattens them into a joint_permissions table per role-and-entity. The rebuild is surgical: rebuildForEntity, L54 regenerates rows for one entity plus its parent chain, and it is triggered from the models themselves — Entity::rebuildPermissions() at Entity, L395 fires inside BaseRepo::create() at BaseRepo, L64 and inside publishDraft() at PageRepo, L94. At read time, EntityPermissionEvaluator::evaluateEntityForUser, L17 collects the page→chapter→book chain built by gatherEntityChainTypeIds() at L139 and resolves explicit allow/deny versus implicit fallback at L35. Listing queries never evaluate in PHP at all — they join the cache with the havingRaw('status IN (1, 3)...') filter shown earlier. Drafts get their own guard: restrictDraftsOnPageQuery() at PermissionApplicator, L117 keeps update drafts invisible to everyone except their author, layered into every page listing.

Search: A Hand-Rolled Scored Index That Replaced MySQL FULLTEXT

The 2017 migration is the confession: create_search_index_table builds the custom search_terms table at migration, L15 and then drops the old FULLTEXT search(...) indexes on pages, books and chapters at L28 — BookStack stopped trusting MySQL relevance ranking and rolled its own. Indexing scores each term: heading elements weight h1 at 10× down to h6 at 1.5× (SearchIndex, L148), tag names get 3× and values 5× (L192), and the entity name is multiplied by 40× at L250. Query time is equally explicit: applyTermSearch() at SearchRunner, L166 builds a subquery over search_terms with prefix LIKE matches, and selectForScoredTerms() at L207 walks backwards to assemble a nested IF(term like ?, score * ..., ...) chain wrapped in SUM(...) at L221. It even adjusts for rarity — getTermAdjustments() at L233 counts term frequency and down-weights common words. Tokenization is custom as well: the delimiter set at SearchIndex, L19 splits on whitespace and punctuation, while the “soft delimiters” .- at L25 mean hyphenated compounds get indexed both whole and split, so a query for either half still hits. Everything stays inside plain SQL so the whole thing runs on stock MySQL or MariaDB.

Revisions, Activity and PDF Export

Every content change snapshots first. PageRepo::update() increments revision_count at PageRepo, L132 and calls RevisionRepo when HTML, name, Markdown or a changelog actually changed at L143. The revision number is collision-safe too: storeNewForPage() takes the max of the page’s count and any in-flight update draft’s version at RevisionRepo, L34, so concurrent drafts cannot fork the sequence. Pruning is configurable: deleteOldRevisions() respects config('app.revision_limit') at RevisionRepo, L49, which defaults to 100 via env('REVISION_LIMIT', 100) in app/Config/app.php, L28. Activity is a first-class domain: ActivityLogger::add() at ActivityLogger, L27 persists an Activity row with user and IP, flashes a session notification, and fans out to webhooks — DispatchWebhookJob implements ShouldQueue at DispatchWebhookJob, L20, so webhook delivery never blocks a save. The constants tell the story of what is tracked: PAGE_CREATE and PAGE_UPDATE at ActivityType, L7. Export is equally layered: PdfGenerator at PdfGenerator, L36 picks between three engines — a custom shell command if exports.pdf_command is set, WKHTML via Snappy only when untrusted fetching is explicitly allowed, and otherwise DomPDF, the zero-configuration default, rendered at L59.

From Laravel Scaffold to Self-Hosted Wiki: Build Facts

Reading composer.json explains a lot of the design. The app targets PHP 8.3+ and Laravel 13, but the dependency list is deliberately short for something this featureful: dompdf/dompdf for default PDF output, league/commonmark for Markdown, ssddanbrown/htmldiff for revision diffs, ezyang/htmlpurifier plus xemlock/htmlpurifier-html5 for sanitizing stored HTML, and knplabs/knp-snappy only as the optional WKHTML bridge. There is no SPA framework — routes/web.php, L34 serves server-rendered Blade views, which is why a single VPS with PHP and MySQL is the entire deployment story. Extensibility comes from the theming system rather than plugins: ThemeService maintains a listener registry with listen() and dispatch() at ThemeService, L36, and named events like PAGE_CONTENT_PRE_STORE and COMMONMARK_ENVIRONMENT_CONFIGURE are fired from inside the content-normalization code you saw above — meaning a theme can rewrite page HTML before it ever touches the database.

Honest Limits

Everything above is verifiable in the repository, but so are the trade-offs. Search indexing rewrites all terms for an entity on every save — indexEntity() deletes then re-inserts (SearchIndex, L35) with 500-row chunks (L112) — so there is no incremental diffing for large pages. A full permission rebuild is chunked but unbounded in scope: rebuildForAll, L32 processes every role against every book and shelf, and it runs synchronously during entity saves rather than on a queue. Activity rows are written inline in the request (ActivityLogger, L39); only webhooks are queued. And the WKHTML PDF engine is intentionally crippled — getActiveEngine() requires allow_untrusted_server_fetching === true before selecting it at PdfGenerator, L42 — because fetching remote resources during PDF rendering is an SSRF risk the developers chose to default away from.
entry.summary: BookStack source tour: how the Laravel wiki organizes Books, Chapters and Pages, scores its own search index, caches permissions, and exports PDFs.

entry.title: How Calibre Works: Inside the E-Book Manager Architecture

link.title: How Calibre Works: Inside the E-Book Manager Architecture

entry.content:
Every e-reader speaks its own dialect: a Kindle wants AZW3, a Kobo prefers EPUB with covers it re-derives itself, and a PDF refuses to reflow on all of them. Metadata is worse — the title lives inside one format’s binary header, the author sort in a sidecar file, the cover wherever that format happens to store it. Calibre’s answer is architectural, not incremental: every imported book becomes a row in one SQLite database, every format conversion funnels through one normalized internal book representation, and one Qt desktop shell drives the whole thing. That is why a twenty-year-old Python application still opens a hundred-thousand-title library without flinching.

This post is a source tour of kovidgoyal/calibre at master. The overview diagram maps the six subsystems that matter: Qt shell, SQLite library, conversion engine, plugin system, content server, device drivers. The detail diagram goes one level deeper into 29 concrete files and the 40 call paths between them.

By the end you will know where metadata.db gets its schema and its collations, how a MOBI file becomes an EPUB without either format knowing the other exists, why the content server is a hand-written HTTP implementation rather than a framework, how USB reader detection and eject actually work, and where the plugin seams are that make all of it extensible.

Calibre at a glance: one Qt shell drives four subsystems over a single SQLite library, and the plugin registry is the seam every one of them resolves components through.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Main, L121 is more than a window: initialize (L248) binds the database, all toolbar actions, the device manager and the library views into one process, and start_content_server (L563) runs the web server inside the same GUI process on demand.
  • Cache, L209 is the library’s public API. Every access passes through the api decorator family (api, L113; read_api, L118; write_api, L123), which takes a read/write lock and touches an in-memory mirror of the data — that mirror is why sorting and searching tens of thousands of rows feels instant.
  • DB, L694 owns the file itself. Its Connection (L511) subclasses apsw.Connection — apsw is a thin CPython C-extension binding that hugs SQLite’s C API closely, the layering covered in our CPython internals tour — sets its pragmas at startup (L526) and registers a custom icucollate collation (L537) so author names sort the way humans expect.
  • construct_path_name, L1888 reveals the on-disk layout: books live as Author/Title (id) directories — the ({}) suffix comes from BOOK_ID_PATH_TEMPLATE, L19, and the joined result is returned at L1907 — so filesystem and database never disagree about where a format file sits.
  • Plumber, L103 is the conversion engine. Its run method (L1224) resolves an input and an output plugin (L957), asks the input side to produce a normalized OEBBook via create_oebbook (L1510), then hands it to output_plugin.convert (L1491).
  • plugin_for_input_format, L676 shows how components are resolved: initialize_plugins (L884) instantiates every builtin and user plugin once at startup, and format lookup is a scan of that registry — 23 input and 17 output format plugins ship in the tree at HEAD.
  • ServerLoop, L425 is the content server’s core: a hand-written HTTP loop multiplexing sockets with select() (L659), wrapping each client in a Connection state machine (L190). There is no web framework import anywhere in the server package.
  • DeviceManager, L233 is a daemon thread that repeatedly calls detect_device (L377), matching USB fingerprints from DeviceScanner, L199 against driver classes until one claims the hardware.
  • viewer main, L214 launches the reader as a separate process with single-instance messaging (L97); before a book opens, prepare_book (L243, convert_book.py) converts non-web formats in pooled worker processes (do_convert, L213) and caches the result by file hash.

The detail view: 29 files, 40 edges. Everything converges on Cache — GUI, content server and viewer all touch the library through the same object, never through raw SQL.

One Library, One SQLite File

A calibre library is just a directory plus metadata.db. When a backend is constructed, DB.__init__ (L704) computes self.dbpath as the join of library_path and metadata.db (L720) and opens or creates the file. Calibre deliberately skips Python’s built-in sqlite3 module here and uses apsw, a lower-level binding with fewer opinionated abstractions on top of SQLite’s C interface — the engine underneath is the same one we dug into in the SQLite source tour.

The schema is versioned by SQLite’s own user_version pragma: DB.user_version (L1843) reads and writes it, and upgrades run stepwise on open. Calibre also pushes real logic into the database: custom aggregate functions like Concatenate (L294) and SortedConcatenate (L315) build author strings inside SQL, and the case-insensitive pynocase (L265) plus ICU-backed icucollate (L285) collators handle text ordering across languages.

The important twist is that the database is not the whole truth at runtime. Cache (L209, cache.py) loads tables into memory and serves reads from there; writes go to SQLite first, then update the mirror. On-disk layout is part of the contract: PathTable.set_path (L173/L174, tables.py) writes the books.path column (L176), and update_path (L2370, backend.py) recomputes it whenever title or author changes, renaming the actual format files on disk in the same operation. format_abspath (L2029) is the resolver that turns a row into a real file path.

This is an embedded, file-per-library design — the opposite pole from a client-server engine like PostgreSQL. There is no daemon, no port, no user management to forget; backing up a library means copying a folder. The price is that calibre owns concurrency itself: read/write locking around Cache, per-connection pragmas, and retry helpers exist because two processes may touch the same library directory at once.

The Conversion Chain: 23 Inputs, 17 Outputs, One Hub

The conversion engine has exactly two plugin contracts. An InputFormatPlugin (L172, conversion.py) implements convert (L247), which receives the source bytes and returns either an OEBBook or HTML — it never learns what the target format will be. An OutputFormatPlugin (L330) implements convert (L380), which receives the OEB object and writes the output file. EPUBOutput, L82 declares file_type = 'epub' (L88), carries an EPUB 2/3 version switch (L158), and builds its ZIP container in create_container (L370); MOBI, AZW3, PDF and DOCX plugins do the same on their side.

Everything in between happens inside Plumber.run (L1224): structure detection (L1362), cleaning (L1344), metadata merging (L1356), plus optional font embedding and subsetting. The OEB book object is the universal currency — because 23 input formats normalize into it and 17 output formats consume it, supporting a new format means writing one plugin file under ebooks/conversion/plugins/, nothing else. Resolution is registry work: plugin_for_input_format (L676) and plugin_for_output_format (L708) scan the initialized plugin list for a matching file_type.

The Content Server: HTTP Without a Framework

The calibre-server entry point builds two objects: Server (L82, standalone.py) constructs a Handler and a ServerLoop (L103). The loop (L425, loop.py) accepts sockets itself, multiplexes them with select() (L659), and hands parsed requests to the handler on a worker pool. Routing is its own tiny layer: the endpoint() decorator (L125, routes.py) wraps plain Python functions taking a Context and RequestData, and Router (L294) matches path patterns with {variables} against its route table.

The handler layer is where server meets library. Context (L40, handler.py) resolves which library a request talks to through get_library (L97), backed by LibraryBroker, L102, which opens and caches one Cache per library id. Long work — conversions, metadata downloads — goes through start_job (L65) instead of blocking the socket, and when a web client edits metadata, notify_changes (L61) pushes the event back toward any listening GUI. Content endpoints in content.py stream covers and book files with content-type sandboxing (needs_sandboxing, L237) so a malicious “book” cannot serve scripts from the server’s origin.

The GUI reuses this exact server in-process (start_content_server, L563) — there is no separate server edition of the library logic, so a change made from a phone browser shows up in the desktop app live.

Devices, the Viewer, and the Plugin Seams

Device support is plugin-driven too. DevicePlugin (L72, interface.py) defines the driver contract: is_usb_connected (L209) answers presence checks, detect_managed_devices (L257) claims hardware, open (L340) initializes it, eject (L368) unmounts it, and post_yank_cleanup (L378) handles the case where you just pulled the cable. DeviceScanner (L199, scanner.py) enumerates candidates through a libusb binding (L73) or Linux sysfs (L114) depending on platform. The USBMS base class (L192, usbms/driver.py) implements the whole mass-storage flow — books (L340) and upload_books (L469) — so vendor drivers only declare IDs, paths and quirks.

The viewer is its own process (main, L214, viewer/main.py), built on QtWebEngine with a custom URL scheme handler (L160, web_view.py). Its trick is the format cache: prepare_book (L243, convert_book.py) keeps a hash-keyed cache of converted copies produced by pooled worker processes (create_worker, L187), so an AZW3 book converts once and re-renders instantly afterwards. Those do_convert workers (L213) speak the same plugin contracts as the desktop app.
