And because everything above is a Plugin subclass (L62, customize/__init__.py) — including device drivers — the customization layer cuts across all of it: load_plugin (L98, customize/ui.py) installs ZIP plugins at runtime, FileTypePlugin.run (L419) fires on import and conversion events, and run_plugins_on_postimport (L293) is the hook the add-books flow calls.

From sqlite3 to apsw: The Rewrites That Built Today’s Calibre

The tree keeps the archaeology visible. The 2008-era v1 backend still ships at library/database.py — docstring: storage of ebooks in an sqlite database — and it imports Python’s sqlite3 directly. The v2 era lives beside it in library/database2.py. Today’s engine is the db/ package: backend.py on apsw plus cache.py in memory, with db/legacy.py providing the compatibility bridge — its create_backend (L59) wires the new pair together and LibraryDatabase (L233) exposes the old API so a decade of GUI code keeps working while it migrates.

The content server was rebuilt the same way. The old library/server package is gone from the tree entirely; src/calibre/srv/ is a from-scratch implementation with no HTTP framework dependency. The format plugin set has grown to 23 input and 17 output plugins at HEAD, and the storage layout — Author/Title (id) directories, id suffix defined in one constant (L19, db/constants.py) — has stayed stable across both rewrites, which is why old libraries still open.

Honest Limits

Everything cited above was verified by reading the source tree at master (commit 8d119ee9e310, checked 2026-11-17); line numbers drift as the code moves. The tour is static analysis: no conversion runs, no server benchmarks, no viewer profiling. Several subsystems were left out on purpose — the news recipe engine, the metadata download sources under ebooks/metadata/sources/, full-text search (db/fts), the notes system (db/notes), the MTP driver path (devices/mtp), and server users and authentication (srv/users.py, srv/auth.py). The C-extension layer (calibre_extensions, library/sqlite_custom.c) is referenced but its build system is not covered. Performance claims reflect design intent in the code — in-memory caching, worker pools — not measured numbers.
entry.summary: How Calibre works: the metadata.db SQLite library, the format conversion engine, the hand-written content server, USB device drivers and the plugin system.

entry.title: How Jitsi Meet Works: Inside the Open-Source Video Conference Architecture

link.title: How Jitsi Meet Works: Inside the Open-Source Video Conference Architecture

entry.content:
Zoom’s free tier cuts group calls off at 40 minutes and gates recordings, custom branding, and admin controls behind paid plans; Microsoft Teams assumes a corporate tenant before it even shows you a join button. Jitsi Meet makes the opposite trade: the entire conferencing frontend is open source, meetings are unlimited, and when you self-host it, every audio and video stream can terminate on your own server instead of a vendor’s region. A hobby project and a school district can run the exact same software.

The catch is that “just read the source” has become misleading advice for this repo. The historic layout everyone blogged about is gone: modules/RTC and modules/XMPP no longer exist, and lib-jitsi-meet — the media and signaling library — now ships as a prebuilt npm artifact loaded from GitHub releases. What remains in jitsi/jitsi-meet is a React + Redux frontend that configures, drives, and observes that library. I walked the current master tree and mapped it into two interactive diagrams: an overview from page load to embedded iframe, and a 33-file detail map covering bootstrap, XMPP connection, the join lifecycle, quality control, rendering, and the embedding API.

By the end of this tour you will be able to trace how a URL like meet.example.com/MyRoom becomes an XMPP connection and a joined conference, where the code decides how many remote videos your browser actually pulls, how the same core drives the Android and iOS apps, and how the iframe API turns a full conference UI into something you embed in your own page.

Overview of the Jitsi Meet web frontend: browser entry on the left, the React shell and single Redux store in the middle, the lib-jitsi-meet bridge and quality control on the right, with the embedding API wrapping it all. Every node links into the live GitHub source.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Two bundles, one global contract. index.html, L86 requires lib-jitsi-meet.min.js and app.bundle.min.js before anything boots — the media/signaling library and the UI are separate deliverables, and the page fails loudly if either is missing.
  • A legacy global still rules. app.js, L57 pins window.APP = {API, conference, UI}; React components, old jQuery-era modules, and the embedding API all communicate through this shared handle.
  • One store, many middlewares. BaseApp.tsx, L257 builds the single Redux store with every feature middleware composed in, then dispatches appWillMount, L115 as the first action.
  • URL in, room out. appNavigate, L41 parses the room URI, awaits loadConfig for the target domain, and dispatches setConfig and setRoom — the room name never lives in a component, only in the store.
  • Connection first, conference second. _connectInternal, L222 news up JitsiMeetJS.JitsiConnection(appId, jwt, options) and registers listeners for CONNECTION_ESTABLISHED, CONNECTION_FAILED, and redirect events before calling connection.connect().
  • The room is created against the connection. _createRoom, L1053 calls APP.connection.initJitsiConference(roomName, options), and room.join, L355 finally sends the presence that joins the XMPP MUC.
  • Quality is a Redux computation. The LastN middleware, L45 prefers startLastN, then channelLastN, then -1, forces 0 in audio-only mode and 1 with a collapsed filmstrip; the video-quality subscriber folds that into receiverConstraints carrying lastN, L407.
  • Embeddable by design. The JitsiMeetExternalAPI constructor, L292 is the public contract: it builds the iframe, wires executeCommand (L1054) and addEventListener (L886) over postMessage, and dispose() tears it all down.

The detail map: 33 files across eight subsystems, from the `createStore` call in BaseApp down to `LargeVideoManager.js` and the postMessage transport behind the iframe API.

Bootstrapping: two bundles and a shared global

The web app is really three layers stacked in one browser tab. The bottom layer is the prebuilt lib-jitsi-meet bundle, which exposes a JitsiMeetJS global; the repo’s lib-jitsi-meet wrapper, L13 re-exports that global as typed constants — JitsiConferenceEvents, JitsiConnectionEvents, track errors — so the rest of the codebase never touches a bare string event name. The middle layer is the React tree: index.web.js, L82 exposes renderEntryPoint, and that call mounts <App> from react/features/app into the page. The top layer is legacy glue: app.js and the 89 KB conference.js, which still own the web join flow.

Once BaseApp mounts, appWillMount, L27 initializes APP.API — the embedding surface must exist before any component can notify a parent page. Then initLib, L50 calls JitsiMeetJS.init(config) with the loaded deployment config, bracketed by LIB_WILL_INIT and LIB_DID_INIT actions. Every feature module under react/features follows the same TypeScript discipline of action types, reducers, and middleware — the same pattern we traced inside the TypeScript compiler itself in our TypeScript source tour, just applied to a Redux app instead of a compiler.

From URL to XMPP connection to a joined conference

The join flow is the best part of this architecture because it shows Redux and the imperative library cooperating. appNavigate, L93 resolves config and sets the room. conference.js init() then dispatches connect() — the web wrapper that reaches _connectInternal, L215. That thunk builds the JitsiConnection, subscribes to connection events (L229–L246), and resolves only on CONNECTION_ESTABLISHED, at which point connectionEstablished, L312 lands in the store with a connect-duration timestamp.

Here is the nuance most descriptions miss. The generic handler _connectionEstablished, L585 dispatches createConference(), L606 — but only when typeof APP === 'undefined', which is the mobile and SDK path; the code even carries a FIXME admitting the web version is handled by conference.js. On web, _createRoom grabs APP.connection (installed by the connection middleware, L23) and creates the JitsiConference imperatively. The portable createConference, L644 does the same trio — initJitsiConference, _addConferenceListeners, sendLocalParticipant — before conference.join(password), L659.

Local media enters the same store. createLocalTracksA, L154 wraps getUserMedia per device, and trackAdded, L407 publishes each JitsiTrack into base/tracks with pending flags so the UI can show spinners while GUM is still running. The conference reducer is a genuine little state machine: joining, L46 holds the conference while it joins, and _conferenceWillJoin / _conferenceJoined move it to the live conference slot (L652, L527). Failure handling lives in the middleware too — CONFERENCE_RESTARTED, max-users, auth errors, and offer/answer failures each get their own recovery branch at _conferenceFailed, L206.

Quality control: LastN, receiver constraints, and assumed bandwidth

Video conferencing quality is mostly a problem of restraint: do not pull what you cannot display. The lastn middleware, L25 recomputes the desired visible stream count whenever the app state, low-bandwidth mode, car mode, filmstrip visibility, or virtual screenshares change — debounced so it fires at most once per second (L74). Its preference chain is explicit: startLastN, then channelLastN, then unlimited (-1); audio-only mode drops it to 0 unless a pinned screenshare deserves 1 (L51–L64).

The video-quality subscriber, L84 listens to the lastN slice, the visible filmstrip participants, the on-stage participant, and the track array, then rebuilds the full receiver-constraints object: per-source maxHeight values plus lastN, dispatched over the bridge data channel via conference.setReceiverConstraints, L512. The sender side is capped too — setSenderVideoConstraint, L362 tells the bridge how much resolution this client uploads, and setVideoQuality clamps user requests to MAX_VIDEO_QUALITY (actions.ts, L125). A maxFullResolutionParticipants config (default 2) downgrades thumbnails to 180p once enough people are on screen (L201).

External parties can shape this too. The iframe command set-assumed-bandwidth-bps (external_api.js, L67) lands in API.js, L428 as a redux dispatch, and the conference middleware forwards it to conference.setAssumedBandwidthBps, L1094 — the estimator input the library uses before the first real bandwidth measurement arrives. When the network degrades anyway, the media-connectivity middleware, L73 listens for MEDIA_CONNECTIVITY_CHANGED and surfaces at-risk, degraded, failed, or interrupted states as notifications, with a five-second damping delay so P2P handovers do not flash warnings (L17).

Rendering: React state drives a legacy layout engine

Who goes on stage is a redux decision. selectParticipantInLargeVideo, L33 resolves the on-stage participant from dominant-speaker and pinned state, but the actual DOM work on web still happens in the old UI layer: subscriber.web.ts, L14 imports VideoLayout from modules/UI/videolayout and calls updateLargeVideo on every relevant state change. That module owns a LargeVideoManager instance, L44, reacts to lastN endpoint churn, L119 so thumbnails entering or leaving the LastN window are re-attached, and delegates per-participant attachment to LargeVideoManager, L468. React computes; the legacy engine paints. On React Native the same state feeds a different component tree under react/features/base/media/components/native — nothing about the join or quality logic is duplicated.

From browser-only to everywhere: React Native and the iframe API

The mobile apps are not a fork. index.ios.js and index.android.js are one-line imports of index.native.js, L35, which registers the same App component tree with React Native’s AppRegistry — the base features, reducers, and the lib-jitsi-meet bridge are shared verbatim, with actions.native.ts / middleware.native.ts variants only where the platform differs. The whole thing builds through npm scripts and webpack on Node.js, and the platform split is enforced by TypeScript file suffixes (.native.ts vs .web.ts) resolved at bundle time.

Embedding follows the same shape in reverse. The JitsiMeetExternalAPI class, L255 creates the iframe (_createIFrame, L375), maps roughly eighty commands and dozens of events (L30, L114), and forwards executeCommand calls into the page (L1054). Inside the page, initCommands, L211 registers handlers that turn each message into a real redux dispatch — so an external setTileView is indistinguishable from a user click — while the external-api middleware, L52 pushes APP.API.notify* messages back out on every dominant-speaker, join, or feedback event. Your host page and the conference UI share one store, two processes apart.

Honest Limits

  • This repo is the frontend only. The SFU that actually forwards media is jitsi-videobridge, the conference focus is jicofo, the XMPP server is prosody, and recording is jibri — all sibling repos. Nothing here implements forwarding, transcoding, or recording — only config plumbing and event handling.
  • No Redis anywhere. Some Jitsi server-side components use Redis, but a case-insensitive scan of this tree finds zero references; the browser client talks XMPP and bridge protocols exclusively.
  • Two UI eras coexist. modules/UI is the pre-React DOM layout that still paints the large video on web; the React subscribers reach into it via direct imports. The replacement is unfinished, which is why conference.js still owns the web join path.
  • The library is external. Symbol names like JitsiConference and JitsiTrack resolve inside the lib-jitsi-meet artifact, not this tree — reading this repo alone shows you the driver’s seat, not the engine.
  • Self-hosting is the real unlock. Unlimited minutes and private media come from pairing this frontend with your own videobridge and prosody; if that itch is what brought you here, we took the same source-level approach for Jellyfin in our Jellyfin source tour.

The overall lesson is architectural: Jitsi Meet treats React as a state coordinator, pushes every irreversible action — connect, join, subscribe, mute — through Redux middleware onto a well-defined external library, and keeps a clean postMessage seam so the same system can be embedded or rendered on a phone.
entry.summary: How the Jitsi Meet frontend works: React conference UI, Redux middleware, the lib-jitsi-meet bridge, LastN video control, and the iframe API, with source maps.

entry.title: How Joplin Works: Inside the Open-Source Note App Architecture

link.title: How Joplin Works: Inside the Open-Source Note App Architecture

entry.content:
If your notes live in a proprietary cloud app, two things are true at once: you pay a monthly fee for the privilege of reading your own words, and getting them out means converting away from a private container format the vendor controls. Cloud note apps lock your notes in proprietary formats and charge monthly — Joplin keeps every note in open Markdown on SQLite and syncs to wherever you want: a local folder, a WebDAV or Nextcloud server, OneDrive, Dropbox, or the project’s own hosted cloud. It is free, open source under AGPL-3.0-or-later, and written entirely in TypeScript, which means every architectural decision is sitting in the repo waiting to be read.

This post is a guided tour of the laurent22/joplin source tree (default branch dev). The two diagrams below were generated from the actual repository structure: the overview shows how three frontends — desktop, terminal CLI, and a self-hostable server — all lean on one shared core library, and the detail diagram zooms into the SQLite storage layer, the sync engine with its FileApi adapters, the markdown-it rendering rules, and the plugin sandbox. Every node links to the real source file on GitHub, so you can jump straight from picture to code.

By the end you will know exactly how a note travels: keystroke in a React editor, row in a SQLite table, serialized item in a three-phase sync loop, rendered HTML on screen — and how third-party plugins hook into all of it without ever getting direct access to your database.

Joplin at a glance — three frontends extend one BaseApplication, all data flows through BaseItem models onto SQLite, and the Synchronizer pushes changes to interchangeable sync targets through a common FileApi.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • One BaseApplication, three frontends. The shared bootstrap lives at BaseApplication, L104 and the desktop app extends it at Application, L85 — window management, auto-update checks and Redux wiring all hang off that single start() at L818.
  • Notes are rows, not files. The Note, L72 model stores the raw Markdown body as a column value; Note.save, L966 is the single write path every frontend uses.
  • Everything syncable funnels through BaseItem. BaseItem, L63 is the parent of notes, folders, resources and tags; its serializeForSync, L527 flattens any item into the text format the sync layer uploads.
  • The sync engine is a three-step loop. Synchronizer, L87 — the comment above start, L404 documents the phases verbatim: UPLOAD, DELETE_REMOTE, DELTA, driven by the syncSteps array at L420.
  • Concurrent clients coordinate with locks. Before touching the remote, the engine calls acquireLock at L632 and auto-refreshes the lease at L634 — two laptops syncing to the same folder cannot corrupt each other.
  • Sync targets are pluggable adapters. BaseSyncTarget, L13 defines the contract; concrete targets include SyncTargetJoplinCloud, L16, SyncTargetOneDrive, L11, SyncTargetWebDAV, L17 and SyncTargetFilesystem, L8.
  • Markdown rendering is markdown-it plus app-aware rules. MdToHtml, L217 keeps a rule table at L42 — fence, KaTeX, mermaid, checkboxes — and registers each one into markdown-it in the merge loop at L599.
  • Plugins run sandboxed against a promise-based API. Plugins call register, L32 with an onStart handler; on desktop their code executes in an isolated iframe behind PluginRunner, L92, never in the main process.

The detail view: the desktop and CLI applications share the Redux reducer and settings model, the database layer offers two SQLite drivers, SearchEngine maintains an FTS4 index beside the tables, and the plugin framework isolates plugin code in a sandbox while exposing the JoplinPlugins API.

One shared core, three frontends

Joplin’s most consequential decision is the shape of packages/lib. It contains the models, the database wrapper, the synchronizer, the settings system and the plugin services, and every frontend imports it as @joplin/lib/.... The desktop UI’s main screen imports the shared reducer directly (MainScreen.tsx, L12), which is why a sidebar click and a CLI command end up mutating the same state shape.

The React layer is a classic Electron split: packages/app-desktop/app.ts runs in the main process (the Application class at L85), while MainScreenComponent at L96 renders the resizable layout and is glued to Redux with connect(mapStateToProps) at L519. The terminal app reuses the same BaseApplication from app-cli/app/app.ts, L28, swapping React for a text GUI — new AppGui(...) at L442 builds a status bar whose prompt() at app-gui.ts, L145 accepts ex-command-style input. Joplin Server, the self-hosted backend in packages/server, is an Express app that ends its boot with app.listen(config().port) at app.ts, L396 and ships its own schema.sqlite. If you enjoy this kind of repo mapping for TypeScript projects, the method transfers almost unchanged to other codebases — see /typescript-source/.

Notes live in SQLite, not a proprietary blob

The storage layer is refreshingly boring, in the best sense. packages/lib/database.ts wraps a single SQLite file: the Database class at L14 creates and migrates tables from a CREATE TABLE _TABLE_NAME_(_FIELDS_TYPE_) template at L363. Two drivers plug in underneath: DatabaseDriverNode at L17 uses the Node sqlite API via shim.nodeSqlite() at L22, while the better-sqlite3 driver at L38 exists as an alternative — its own header comments explain the trade-off around SQLITE_DQS=0.

Each entity is a plain model: Note, L72, Folder, L45 with a notebook tree rebuilt by allAsTree at L902, and Resource, L58 for attachments — binaries stay on disk as files, with only metadata in the table. Search is handled by SearchEngine at services/search/SearchEngine.ts, L97, which mirrors notes into an notes_fts FTS4 table (see the count(*) query at L359 and the matchinfo comments at L378). Because the store is a real relational database with a published schema, you can query your notes with any SQLite client — the notes are yours at the file level, not behind an API. The design contrasts nicely with server-only stores; for the fundamentals of that storage engine, see /sqlite/.

The Synchronizer: upload, delete_remote, delta

Synchronization is where Joplin earns its “your notes, anywhere” claim. Synchronizer.start() at L404 executes three phases, named in the code itself at L401–403: upload items changed locally since the last sync, delete_remote items deleted locally, and delta — pull remote changes by listing the target and applying differences. The step list is configurable at L420, and partial syncs skip the delta phase.

Because several devices may point at the same storage, the engine takes a sync lock before doing anything: this.lockHandler().acquireLock(LockType.Sync, ...) at L632, then starts auto-refreshing the lease at L634 so a long sync is not evicted mid-flight; a stuck lock from a dead client expires via TTL. The lock machinery itself is LockHandler at services/synchronizer/LockHandler.ts, L146. Items cross the wire as the flat text produced by serializeForSync at L527, and any item that cannot sync (an oversized resource, for instance) is flagged in the sync_disabled bookkeeping written by updateSyncTimeQueries at L920.

What makes the design durable is that the engine only talks to a FileApi — the abstraction at file-api.ts, L165 with put/get/list operations — and each backend implements it. The packages/lib folder ships eleven SyncTarget*.ts classes: Joplin Cloud and Joplin Server (including a SAML variant), OneDrive, Dropbox, WebDAV, Nextcloud (a WebDAV preset), the local file system, plus memory and no-op targets used in tests. Optional end-to-end encryption wraps the payloads in EncryptionService at services/e2ee/EncryptionService.ts, L89 — encryptFile at L744 and encryptString at L730 — so even a WebDAV folder you don’t control only ever stores ciphertext.

How markdown becomes HTML — and where plugins run

Rendering is a markdown-it wrapper with opinions. MdToHtml at L217 implements the MarkupRenderer interface and exposes render() at L462. Its rules table at L42–58 maps rule names to modules in MdToHtml/rules/: fenced code handling, KaTeX math, mermaid diagrams, checkboxes, images, sanitization. Each rule module exports a markdown-it plugin — the fence rule’s plugin(markdownIt) at rules/fence.ts, L15, KaTeX’s plugin factory at rules/katex.ts, L349. At render time the merge loop at L599 combines built-in and extra rules, skips disabled ones via pluginEnabled, and calls markdownIt.use(plugin, options) at L610 — which is how per-syntax settings like toggling ==mark== become real. A comment block above that loop, at L572–597, is effectively design documentation: it spells out the three ways a markdown plugin can hook in depending on whether it needs app data or toggleable settings.

Plugins get the same courtesy at the application level. PluginService at services/plugins/PluginService.ts, L92 loads packaged plugins and, notably, extracts the manifest from an embedded /* joplin-manifest: comment at L292–307 so a plugin is one script plus its metadata. The API a plugin sees is a tree of Joplin* classes — joplin.plugins.register({...}) at JoplinPlugins.ts, L32 fires the plugin’s onStart and emits started when it resolves. On desktop, execution is not in-process: PluginRunner at app-desktop/services/plugins/PluginRunner.ts, L92 marshals every call through executeSandboxCall (imported at L3) into a sandboxed iframe, so a buggy plugin crashes its own context, not your editor.

From Evernote importer to 27-package monorepo

Joplin started life as a note app with an Evernote import path — packages/lib/import-enex.ts still carries that heritage — but the repo has grown into a yarn-workspaces monorepo: the root package.json declares "workspaces": ["packages/*"] and pins engines to Node >=22.19 and yarn 4.17.0 (the terminal and server packages run on plain Node; for background on that runtime, see /node/). Counting package.json files under packages/ in the current tree yields 27 packages: the four frontends (app-desktop, app-cli, app-mobile, app-clipper), the shared lib, the renderer, the server, a standalone editor, plus support tooling — turndown and two forked libraries for HTML-to-Markdown conversion, an onenote-converter, transcribe and whisper-voice-typing for voice notes, generate-plugin-doc and generator-joplin for the plugin ecosystem, and the tools package that automates builds and translations. The whole tree is licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later by the root LICENSE file. The default branch is dev; every file cited in this post was verified there at commit 68b1f92.

Honest Limits

  • Line numbers drift. All citations reference branch dev at commit 68b1f92; the repository moves fast, so treat links as a snapshot.
  • Coverage is honest about scope. The tour concentrated on packages/lib, packages/app-desktop, packages/app-cli, packages/renderer and packages/server; packages/app-mobile (React Native) shares the same core but was not examined line-by-line here.
  • “Everything is Markdown” has an asterisk. Note bodies default to MarkupLanguage.Markdown, but the renderer family at MarkupToHtml.ts, L26 also carries an HTML source mode, and attachments are binary files referenced from rows — the openness applies to the store and format, not a claim that no other data exists.
  • Search is FTS4, not semantic. The classic path indexes into SQLite FTS4; semantic/embedding search exists alongside it (services/ai/EmbeddingIndexer.ts), but the default search matches on the FTS index.
  • No peer-to-peer sync. The eleven built-in target classes are the complete list; there is no git or P2P transport — extensibility comes from implementing the FileApi contract against a new backend.
entry.summary: How Joplin works: Electron/React desktop app, SQLite note store, the Synchronizer with pluggable sync targets, terminal CLI, plugin API, markdown-it rendering.

entry.title: How Logseq Works: Inside the Outliner and Datascript Architecture

link.title: How Logseq Works: Inside the Outliner and Datascript Architecture

entry.content:
Roam Research popularized networked note-taking — daily journals, bidirectional links, blocks you can refactor anywhere — but your knowledge base lives on someone else’s cloud, behind a subscription, in a format you cannot grep. Logseq answers that pain with a different bargain: the same outliner model, but your graph is stored on your own disk, and the entire application that manages it is open source. The current database version goes further than “plain files on disk”: a graph is a single SQLite database you can back up with one file copy, while Markdown export remains a derived, human-readable projection you can generate on demand.

Two diagrams in this post map that bargain onto the actual source tree. The overview traces the life of a keystroke: editor handler → outliner op → DB worker → in-memory Datascript → SQLite file, and back to the screen as immutable snapshots. The detail diagram adds the boot sequence, the schema and DataScript layer, the persistence backends (OPFS in the browser, files on the desktop), the query engine, and the plugin/SDK surface.

Reading this tour you will learn how a Lisp dialect (ClojureScript, compiled to JavaScript by shadow-cljs) runs a serious desktop app; why every paragraph you type is really an EDN datom; how the team moved graph ownership out of the renderer into a dedicated worker thread; how Datalog — not SQL, not a REST API — powers advanced queries; and what changed when Logseq migrated from Markdown-folder graphs to the SQLite-backed DB version. Every symbol cited below was verified against the master branch of logseq/logseq.

Overview: a keystroke crosses three boundaries — renderer to op layer, op layer to db worker, worker to SQLite — and returns as a snapshot diff.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • App entry. frontend.core/start, L74 mounts the root React component through the rfx provider; the namespace self-describes as the entry for “the mobile, browser and electron frontend apps” (ns docstring, L2).
  • Boot orchestration. frontend.handler/start!, L142 starts IndexedDB, registers plugin hosting, installs Electron IPC listeners, then kicks off persist-db/<start-runtime!, L171 and graph restore — a genuine “system component” in a codebase that otherwise favors pure functions.
  • The UI–worker bridge. frontend.state/<invoke-db-worker, L66 is the single choke point every renderer thread call takes to reach the worker; it throws immediately if the worker atom is not yet initialized.
  • Editor intent. frontend.handler.editor/save-block!, L1668 sits at the top of the tallest file in the frontend; its job is to translate caret state and user edits into outliner operations, not to touch the database.
  • Semantic ops. frontend.modules.outliner.op/transact!, L166 executes ops accumulated in a dynamic var by builders like save-block!, L36 — so a multi-block edit is one atomic batch, not N writes.
  • Ordered delivery. frontend.db.transact/apply-outliner-ops, L175 ships the batch to the worker as a thread-api request, after enqueue-outliner-mutation!, L26 chained it onto a per-repo promise tail so concurrent edits can never interleave.
  • The worker. frontend.worker.db-worker/init, L30 initializes the graph core inside a browser worker and exposes a Comlink proxy, L43 — the same pattern a REST server uses to own the database while clients render.
  • The database. logseq.db.common.sqlite/get-storage-conn, L23 restores an in-memory Datascript connection whose datoms are persisted through a storage layer backed by SQLite — Datascript for queries, SQLite for durability.
  • Queries. frontend.db.query-dsl/query, L40 shows that even simple query strings execute in the worker, keeping parser cost off the UI thread.

Detail: the same flow with boot, schema, persistence backends, queries and the plugin SDK included — node labels name real namespaces you can open on GitHub.

Why Every Note Is a Datom

Logseq’s core data model is not “pages containing text” — it is a graph of entities whose state is a set of EDN datoms: entity, attribute, value, transaction tuples held in Datascript, an in-memory database that implements the Datalog logic language. The outliner layer validates blocks against an explicit map of the fields that make a block a block: :block/uuid, :block/order, :block/parent and :block/page (block-map, L57). Nesting an outline is literally writing :block/parent datoms; reordering is rewriting :block/order. The same file’s save-block, L672, insert-blocks, L1099 and delete-blocks, L1395 are the primitive verbs of the whole app — everything else, from templates to task lists, compiles down to them.

Because the model is a database, features that other apps bolt on with string matching become queries. “All properties of this page” is an avet-index datom scan: get-all-properties, L42 reads :block/tags datoms directly. Breadcrumbs are a parent walk: get-page-parents, L47. This is the block graph model that made outliner tools famous, expressed as data rather than as a document format — the same philosophy we examined in the Node source tour, where module structure is likewise the primary data, except here even your notes are queryable facts. The batch-txs state, L4 in the outliner dep is where collected ops wait to become one transaction.

The DB Worker Split: Why the Renderer No Longer Owns Your Graph

The most consequential recent decision in this codebase is architectural, not feature-wise: the graph database lives in a dedicated worker thread, and the renderer holds only immutable snapshots. The worker’s entrypoint (init, L30) initializes the database core and exposes it over Comlink; the renderer-side subscription layer calls itself “Immutable renderer snapshots loaded from the worker-owned graph database” (ns docstring, L2) and warms an LRU cache of twenty thousand slots (warm-cache-size, L11) through batched loads like <load-block, L55.

The write path mirrors the read path. The frontend transact namespace serializes each repository’s mutations by chaining promises (enqueue-outliner-mutation!, L26) before transact, L162 dispatches the request; when the worker returns, deltas are applied to the renderer under react-dom/flushSync (publish-worker-response!, L147) so the caret never visibly lags. This split is why heavy operations — full-graph queries, schema restore, undo grouping — stopped janking the editor: they are worker-side by construction. The project records these decisions as ADRs, and the worker also owns undo/redo semantics per those documents.

Startup follows the same ownership rule: restore-graph!, L11 opens the graph “from SQLite” (docstring, L12), fetches the schema through the persistence backend, resolves sync conflicts, and only then resets renderer subscriptions. The renderer never loads raw datoms itself — it asks the worker.

Queries: From Query Blocks to Datalog

Logseq ships two query tiers, and both compile down to the database the worker owns. The DSL tier is what you write in query blocks on a page: the renderer namespace is explicitly a thin wrapper, “Query execution belongs to the db worker” (ns docstring, L2); query, L40 dispatches thread-api/query-dsl-query, and the custom-query variant, L52 handles the advanced form.

The advanced tier is real Datalog. The guard require-datalog-query!, L46 rejects anything that is not a proper query vector starting with :find (the :find check, L50), and the namespace titles itself the handler for “custom queries a.k.a. advanced queries” (ns docstring, L2). That means the full expressiveness of Datalog — rule bodies, joins across :block/parent chains — is available inside a note. This is the quiet superpower of storing notes as datoms: a “query” is not a plugin feature, it is the native interface of the storage engine, and Logseq just picks the executing thread.

From Plain-Markdown Folders to SQLite Graphs

This section is the build-facts record of Logseq’s biggest migration. The classic released Logseq — still what most users run — treats a folder of Markdown and Org files as the source of truth: files are parsed by the mldoc parser (a separate Logseq project wrapped in ClojureScript, “taking and returning edn” only, logseq.graph-parser.mldoc, L2) and the AST is turned into transactions during import (graph-parser.extract docstring, L2). In that world, Datascript was rebuilt by re-parsing your files at startup, and sync meant file syncing.

The DB version on master inverts that: the source of truth is a SQLite file, addressed as get-db-full-path, L49 mapping a graph to its db.sqlite, and Datascript datoms persist through a storage table with (addr, content, addresses) rows created by create-kvs-table!, L10 for use with datascript.storage (docstring, L11). Fresh graphs are stamped out by schema helpers in logseq.db.sqlite.create-graph, L2 — built-in classes, properties and typed property values — and graph-kind checks lean on db-version-prefix, L308. The README marks the DB version beta while mobile and real-time collaboration mature (README, L71), and the dependency list wires the pieces together: the Datascript fork (deps.edn, L10), the outliner library (deps.edn, L45) and the db-sync library (deps.edn, L46).

Markdown survives, but demoted to a projection. ADR 0016 specifies an Electron-only mirror that writes derived Markdown under mirror/markdown/journals/ and mirror/markdown/pages/ (ADR 0016) — with the explicit rule that “the DB remains the source of truth” and mirror files feed back into nothing. If you want to understand how a durable local store can back an editor, the SQLite engine behind this design is itself worth a source tour.

Plugins and the Electron Shell

The extension surface is a second ClojureScript namespace reserved for third parties: logseq.api, L2 is documented as “Logseq API for plugins usage” and exports dozens of hooks — slash command registration (register_plugin_slash_command, L53), storage files, user settings, UI items. The host installs during boot via handler.plugin/setup!, L1341. DB-version-specific plugin calls live in logseq.api.db-based, L2 (“DB version related fns”), which routes page and property mutations through the same outliner core the editor uses — plugins get no side door into the database, and block APIs even namespace their properties (plugin.property prefix, L17) to keep plugin data distinguishable from user data. Compared with the compiler-checked, type-first approach we covered in the TypeScript source tour, this is a runtime-gated API: flexible for authors, stricter at the boundary.

On the desktop, the same ClojureScript bundle runs inside Electron. The renderer talks to the main process through electron.ipc/ipc, L28, which serializes payloads as transit strings before calling window.apis.doAction (doAction call, L33) — one typed channel instead of dozens of ad-hoc bridges. The main process owns filesystem primitives (native db.sqlite files, plugin directories, the Markdown mirror), while all content logic stays in the worker per the ADR.

Honest Limits

  • Master is the DB-version branch. The SQLite graph, worker split and mirror ADR describe current master; the classic file-version code paths largely live in release branches and history. Treat master as fast-moving — the README itself steers stability-seekers elsewhere.
  • DB version is beta. The README says data loss is possible and recommends backups; real-time collaboration is in alpha. The sync libraries exist in-tree (db-sync dep, L46) but the surrounding product surface is explicitly unfinished.
  • The Markdown mirror is one-way. Editing mirrored files does not update the graph, per ADR 0016; it is an export, not round-trip sync, and browser/mobile builds do not get it.
  • Datascript is still in memory. Durability comes from the SQLite storage layer, so very large graphs trade RAM for query speed; the kvs-table design (create-kvs-table!, L10) is the boundary where that trade is managed.
  • Docs drift. src/main/frontend/persist_db/README.md still describes the older in-memory mental model, so older tutorials can disagree with newer code about where the database lives.
entry.summary: How Logseq works inside: the ClojureScript outliner frontend, Datascript EDN datoms on SQLite, the DB worker split, Datalog queries and the plugin API.
